events.summary: Chip and AI stocks fell after a Financial Times report that OpenAI's annualized revenue is about $20bn lower than previously reported: OpenAI told investors it was 'nearing $50 billion', against roughly $70bn reported earlier (CNN). Nasdaq -1.25% (worst day since mid-August), S&P 500 -0.5%, Nvidia -2.9%, Intel -5.3%, Oracle -5.5% (CNN). Yahoo's live blog: the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell as much as 4% intraday; Marvell and Arm fell more than 6%; Brent oil above $104 on Middle East tensions and the 10-year Treasury yield at 5.23% added pressure. The chip fund SMH fell 2.84% and Lumentum 5.62% (data/prices). Credo fell 3.70%.
events.why_it_matters: OpenAI is one of the largest buyers of AI computing; lower revenue raises doubts about how fast AI data-center spending can grow, which is what drives Credo's sales (inference, medium). Baird's Ross Mayfield to CNN: 'There are going to be tremors throughout all of the related sub-industries.' Credo's own part of the move was small (+0.71 points, z 0.15).

why_chain.text: Thursday 10-08: Credo fell 3.70% (220.01 to 211.86). Attribution: market -0.45 points, chips industry -3.96, Credo's own +0.71 (z 0.15, normal noise). So Thursday was an industry move, not a Credo story.
Chip and AI stocks fell broadly: Nasdaq -1.25%, the semiconductor index down as much as 4% intraday, Nvidia -2.9%, Marvell and Arm more than -6%; the chip fund SMH -2.84%.

Trigger: a Financial Times report that OpenAI's annualized revenue is 'nearing $50 billion', about $20bn below the roughly $70bn previously reported. Rising oil (Brent above $104) and a 5.23% 10-year Treasury yield added pressure.

Why that hits chip suppliers: OpenAI and the cloud companies building for it are among the biggest buyers of AI data-center hardware; if AI revenue is smaller than thought, investors fear the spending on chips, switches and cables may grow more slowly.
why_chain.evidence: inference (medium); supported by Baird's Ross Mayfield quoted by CNN: 'tremors throughout all of the related sub-industries'

why_chain.text: Basic driver: AI-hardware share prices rest on expected future data-center spending, which in the end must be paid for by AI revenue. News that this revenue is lower lowers that expectation for the whole group, Credo included.
Friday 10-09: Credo rose 2.21% while SMH fell 0.65%. Attribution: market +0.66, industry -2.02, Credo's own +3.57 (z 0.75, normal noise).

Optical stocks rebounded after Lumentum's CEO said optical components are 'completely sold out through early 2029' (Lumentum closed +5.22%). Credo now sells optical products too, so its own part of the move most likely came from this group rebound, which SMH does not capture.
Credo's OCP Summit press release came out before Friday's open, but it contains no numbers; any effect on the price is unknown.
Net over the two days: -1.57%, with the industry part -5.90 and Credo's own part +4.13 (z 0.62): Credo held up better than chip stocks generally.

products.name: 1.6T ZeroFlap Active Light Cable (ALC) and ZeroFlap optics (shown at OCP 2026)
products.what_it_is: Credo's optical connection products: transceivers (and, from the name, a cable with optics built into its ends) that carry data as light at 1.6 terabits per second. The release read does not define 'Active Light Cable'; the cable description is an inference from the name and from Credo's 'Active Electrical Cable' naming (medium).
products.analogy: If an AEC is a garden hose with a booster pump at each end, an optical cable is a pipe that carries water much further with almost no loss; it costs more and uses more power, so it is used where the hose is too short.
products.buyers: Hyperscale cloud and AI data-center operators (Credo does not name them).
products.how_it_works: A digital signal processor chip (DSP, the 'Cardinal DSP') cleans and times the signal; optics turn it into light. 'ZeroFlap' is Credo's brand for links built to avoid 'link flaps' (brief drops that stall AI training jobs); 'PILOT observability' is Credo's monitoring for the link's health.
products.sales: Not disclosed by product. Proxy (labelled): management guided optical revenue above $600m for fiscal 2027 on the 2026-09 results call (transcript, tier 3), against total Q1 FY2027 revenue of $479.0m.
products.stage: Demonstrated at trade shows; the OCP release gives no shipping or customer status for the ALC. ZeroFlap optics ramp was expected in fiscal Q1 2027 across more than four customers (tier-3 coverage, not verified against a primary source in this run).
products.size_for_company: Optics is the second growth leg; above $600m guided for fiscal 2027 would be a large share of revenue, but the exact split is not disclosed.
products.competition: Broadcom, Marvell and the transceiver makers (Lumentum, Coherent, InnoLight) in optics; tier-3 coverage, not verified this run.
products.why_investors_care: Thesis 2: Credo needs optics to keep growing once speeds and distances outgrow copper.
products.watch_next: Any optical revenue figure or named customer at Q2 FY2027 results (about 2026-12-02, not confirmed); CEO's OCP talk on 10-12.

products.name: Micro-Emitter NPO-enabled optical backplane for scale-up (shown at OCP 2026)
products.what_it_is: An optical 'backplane': the wiring that links many AI chips inside one rack, done with light instead of copper. NPO usually means near-packaged optics, with the light engines placed right next to the chip (general industry meaning; the release text read does not define it).
products.analogy: Replacing the copper wiring inside a building's walls with fibre: much more capacity in the same space.
products.buyers: Builders of large AI racks (cloud companies, AI-system makers); no buyers named.
products.how_it_works: Company claim: a 'high-reliability micro-emitter blind-mate optical backplane architecture' that 'delivers up to 10x higher bandwidth compared to the latest copper backplanes'. 'Blind-mate' means boards plug in without anyone connecting cables by hand.
products.sales: not disclosed; demonstration stage, no revenue reported
products.stage: Demonstration (booth demo 13-15 October 2026); no production or customer status given.
products.competition: not available in sources read this run
products.why_investors_care: It aims at 'scale-up' links inside a rack, a market today served mostly by copper; it could be a future product line, and it shows Credo competing against copper, including its own AECs.
products.watch_next: Whether any customer or timeline is named at OCP (12-15 October) or on the next results call.
